column13: 🎯 THE ROOT CAUSE IS THE DAY'S DEFECT FAMILY ARRIVING IN A THIRD ACTIVITY, AND IT IS THE SHARPEST STATEMENT OF IT YET. OSPREY believed it had fixed the HAW-15 lesson by 'searching the mechanism'. In practice its sweep was still ANCHORED ON AN ENUMERATION -- Novorossiysk, Sheskharis, CPC, Primorsk, Ust-Luga, the facilities it already knew. TAMAN WAS NEVER ON THE LIST, SO IT WAS NOT MISSED FROM IT; IT WAS INVISIBLE TO IT. Every query returned results, nothing errored, and the sweep REPORTED COMPLETE. ⇒ A NAMED-FACILITY LIST IS A CLOSED SET STANDING IN FOR AN OPEN ONE, and the failure is silent by construction because a closed set cannot report what it does not contain. OSPREY's fix is correct and non-obvious: anchor on MECHANISM + GEOGRAPHY (every Russian Black Sea/Azov/Baltic oil-handling port, named or not) with >=1 query per sweep CONTAINING NO FACILITY NAME AT ALL -- because ADDING TAMAN TO THE LIST WOULD BE THE SAME ERROR WITH ONE MORE NAME. ⇒ THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT AS HAW-19'S ENUMERATED LEGS, ONE DAY APART AND IN A DIFFERENT ACTIVITY: an enumerated set is a hidden claim that the enumeration is complete. Mine was legs in a PREDICTION (test design); OSPREY's was names in a SEARCH (evidence gathering). Together with WALTER's scoped-measurement-unscoped-label defect, that is the SAME failure class across TEST DESIGN, EVIDENCE GATHERING and INSTRUMENTATION in a single day. ⚠️ ROUTED: OSPREY warned WALTER that if its registry carries a Russian-facility NAME LIST it has identical exposure. That is the correct generalisation -- the defect lives in the SHAPE of the index, not in any one desk's diligence.
